questions.stem: Energy from the Sun crosses the near-vacuum of space. Which explains that?
options: Conduction, because space contains widely spaced particles that collide
Convection, as hot gas currents circulate outwards from the Sun
Radiation, as very fast mechanical waves that push through empty space
Radiation, as electromagnetic waves, which need no medium of particles
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation is an oscillating electric and magnetic field, so it propagates without any particles to carry it — this is why it is the only one of the three transfer methods that works through a vacuum. Saying radiation is a very fast mechanical wave is tempting because radiation clearly is a wave, but mechanical waves by definition require a medium of particles. The cue is the vacuum: any explanation that needs particles must be wrong.

questions.stem: On a wave diagram, the wavelength is measured as the distance from one crest to the next. What does the amplitude measure?
options: The maximum displacement of the medium from its rest position
The number of complete waves passing a fixed point each second
The distance the wave travels during one complete oscillation
The vertical distance from the top of a crest to the bottom of a trough
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the greatest displacement of a particle (or field) from the undisturbed rest position, and it is linked to the energy the wave carries. The crest-to-trough distance is a very common wrong answer: that distance is actually twice the amplitude, not the amplitude itself. Remember amplitude is measured from the centre line, not across the whole wave.

questions.stem: Which pair of waves is correctly classified?
options: Both sound and microwaves are mechanical waves
Both sound and microwaves are electromagnetic waves
Sound is mechanical; microwaves are electromagnetic
Sound is electromagnetic; microwaves are mechanical
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves are vibrations of particles in a medium, so sound is mechanical and cannot travel through a vacuum; microwaves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum and travel through a vacuum at 3 × 10^8 m/s. Grouping both as electromagnetic is tempting because both are used in communication technology, but a use in technology says nothing about the type of wave. The test is simple: ask whether the wave still travels when all the particles are removed.

questions.stem: A wave in a spring has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.75 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Wave speed equals frequency × wavelength, so 4.0 × 0.75 = 3.0 m/s. The answer 5.3 m/s comes from dividing frequency by wavelength (4.0 ÷ 0.75), a common reversal of the relationship. Check units as you go: hertz (per second) multiplied by metres gives metres per second, which only works for multiplication.

questions.stem: A room heater warms the air near it and the whole room gradually becomes warmer. Which statement correctly describes the convection involved?
options: Warmed air becomes denser and sinks, pushing cool air upwards to form a circulating current
Warmed air rises because hot particles are attracted upwards towards the cooler ceiling
Warmed air expands, becomes less dense and rises, and cooler denser air sinks to take its place
Warmed air particles vibrate faster on the spot and pass energy along by colliding with each other
questions.explanation: Convection happens in fluids: heating makes the air expand so the same mass occupies more volume, lowering its density, and the less dense air is pushed upwards by surrounding denser air, setting up a circulating current. The option about particles vibrating on the spot and colliding describes conduction, which is very slow in gases because the particles are far apart. The cue for convection is bulk movement of the fluid itself, driven by a density difference.

questions.stem: A ray of light travelling through air enters a block of glass, where it slows down. What happens to its frequency and wavelength inside the glass?
options: Frequency increases and wavelength decreases
Frequency stays the same and wavelength decreases
Frequency decreases and wavelength stays the same
Both frequency and wavelength decrease
questions.explanation: The frequency of a wave is set by its source and does not change when the wave enters a new medium, so if speed decreases then wavelength must decrease as well, since speed equals frequency × wavelength. Saying both decrease looks reasonable because the wave has clearly 'slowed', but a change in frequency would mean the colour of the light changed on entering the glass, which does not happen. The rule to remember is: frequency is fixed by the source, wavelength adjusts to the medium.

questions.stem: A 60 W electric globe converts 60 J of electrical energy each second into 5 J of light and 55 J of thermal energy. Which statement about this is correct?
options: Energy is conserved, but 55 J each second is transferred to a less useful form
55 J of energy is destroyed each second, so only 5 J survives as light
Energy is conserved only in the 5 J of light; the thermal energy is lost from the universe
The globe creates 5 J of light energy each second from the 55 J of waste heat
questions.explanation: The law of conservation of energy says energy is not created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed, so all 60 J is still accounted for — it is just that most of it ends up as thermal energy spread into the surroundings rather than as useful light. The statement that 55 J is destroyed is the classic misreading of the everyday word 'lost': in physics, wasted energy is degraded and dispersed, not removed from existence. Whenever you see 'energy lost', translate it as 'energy transferred to a form we cannot use'.

questions.stem: Which list places these electromagnetic waves in order from longest wavelength to shortest?
options: Radio waves, infrared, visible light, X-rays
X-rays, visible light, infrared, radio waves
Infrared, radio waves, X-rays, visible light
Visible light, infrared, radio waves, X-rays
questions.explanation: Across the electromagnetic spectrum, wavelength decreases (and frequency increases) from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. The reversed list starting with X-rays is tempting if you remember the order but not which end is 'longest'. Anchor it with radio: radio waves have the longest wavelengths and the lowest frequencies of the whole spectrum.

questions.stem: A water wave has a speed of 6.0 m/s and a wavelength of 2.4 m. What is its frequency?
options: 0.4 Hz
3.6 Hz
2.5 Hz
questions.explanation: Using speed = frequency × wavelength, frequency = speed ÷ wavelength = 6.0 ÷ 2.4 = 2.5 Hz. The answer 0.4 Hz comes from dividing the wrong way round (2.4 ÷ 6.0), so always check that dividing a speed by a length leaves 'per second'. The value 14.4 Hz comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A vacuum flask keeps hot coffee hot. Its silvered inner surfaces are designed mainly to reduce which type of energy transfer?
options: Radiation, because shiny surfaces reflect infrared radiation back towards the coffee
Conduction, because silver stops particle collisions passing energy through the glass
Convection, because the silver layer prevents currents forming in the liquid
Radiation, because silvered surfaces absorb infrared and store the energy in the metal
questions.explanation: Infrared radiation needs no medium, so the vacuum gap cannot stop it; the silvering reflects that radiation back instead of letting it escape. Blaming conduction is tempting because silver is a good conductor, but that is exactly why silver would be a poor choice for blocking conduction — the vacuum itself deals with conduction and convection. The cue: a vacuum removes particles, so only radiation is left to be handled by the surface finish.

questions.stem: A ball of mass 0.50 kg is dropped and loses 20 J of gravitational potential energy as it falls, but arrives at the ground with only 18 J of kinetic energy. Which statement best applies the law of conservation of energy here?
options: The missing 2 J has been transferred to the surrounding air and ball as thermal energy and sound
The missing 2 J has been destroyed by air resistance, so energy is not conserved in this fall
The ball only converted 18 J because gravitational potential energy is always partly lost in storage
The missing 2 J remains as unconverted potential energy still stored in the ball at ground level
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so any shortfall in kinetic energy must appear in other forms — here, heating of the air and ball through friction, plus a little sound. Saying the energy was destroyed by air resistance is the classic misreading: friction degrades energy into less useful forms, it does not remove it from the universe. Whenever a figure seems 'lost', ask which form it turned into rather than whether it vanished.

questions.stem: Two sound waves travel through the same air. Wave X has twice the amplitude of wave Y, and both have the same frequency. Which comparison is correct?
options: Wave X is louder and travels faster, because larger amplitude means more energy per second
Wave X has a higher pitch than wave Y, because amplitude and pitch increase together
Wave X has a shorter wavelength than wave Y, because a taller wave is squeezed up more
Wave X is louder than wave Y, and both waves travel at the same speed through the air
questions.explanation: Amplitude determines the energy carried and therefore the loudness, while the speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature, not on how loud the sound is. The option adding 'travels faster' is tempting because more energy sounds like it should mean more speed, but a shout and a whisper reach a listener at the same moment. Pitch is set by frequency, which is stated to be identical for both waves, and with equal speed and frequency the wavelengths must also match.

questions.stem: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave. What does that mean?
options: The air particles are carried along with the wave to the listener
The wave travels in a straight line rather than spreading out
The particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the wave's travel
The particles vibrate up and down at right angles to its travel
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave the oscillation of the medium is along the same line as the energy transfer, producing regions of compression and rarefaction. The option describing vibration at right angles defines a transverse wave, such as a wave on a rope. The cue is the word 'longitudinal', meaning 'along': the vibration lies along the travel direction, and the particles oscillate about fixed positions rather than moving with the wave.

questions.stem: A vibrating loudspeaker cone produces 60 complete waves in 4.0 seconds. What is the frequency of the sound?
options: 64 Hz
15 Hz
240 Hz
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of complete waves produced (or passing a point) each second, so it is 60 ÷ 4.0 = 15 Hz. The answer 240 Hz comes from multiplying 60 by 4.0 instead of dividing, which would be the count for 4 seconds repeated each second. Check the units: hertz means 'per second', so the number of waves must be divided by the time in seconds.

questions.stem: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 250 Hz and a wavelength of 1.36 m. What is the speed of the sound?
questions.explanation: Wave speed is found from speed = frequency × wavelength, so 250 × 1.36 = 340 m/s, the usual speed of sound in air. The value 184 m/s comes from dividing 250 by 1.36, reversing the relationship. A quick check is the unit combination: hertz (per second) multiplied by metres gives metres per second, so the two quantities must be multiplied.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg trolley released at the top of a ramp loses 60 J of gravitational potential energy, but arrives at the bottom with only 45 J of kinetic energy. Which statement correctly applies the law of conservation of energy?
options: The missing 15 J was destroyed by friction, showing that energy is only conserved when no friction acts on a moving object
The missing 15 J stayed behind as gravitational potential energy stored in the ramp, and is released when the trolley is lifted again
The trolley converted 15 J of its kinetic energy back into potential energy, which is why it slows down before reaching the bottom
The missing 15 J has been transferred to thermal energy and sound in the ramp, wheels and air, so the total energy is unchanged
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed, so any shortfall in useful kinetic energy has become thermal energy and sound spread through the surroundings. The claim that friction destroys energy is the classic error — friction degrades energy into less useful forms but never removes it from the universe. Whenever a total appears to shrink, look for the 'wasted' thermal and sound outputs rather than concluding energy has vanished.

questions.stem: Microwaves used in communications and X-rays used in medical imaging are both electromagnetic waves travelling through a vacuum. Which comparison is correct?
options: X-rays travel faster because their higher frequency carries more energy per second
Microwaves travel faster because their longer wavelength lets them cover more distance per cycle
Both travel at the same speed, but X-rays have the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength
Both travel at the same speed, but X-rays have the higher frequency and the longer wavelength
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, about 300 000 km/s, so since speed = frequency × wavelength, a higher frequency must be paired with a proportionally shorter wavelength. The option pairing higher frequency with longer wavelength breaks this inverse relationship. The reminder is that in a fixed medium, frequency and wavelength trade off against each other; only the medium can change the speed.

questions.stem: Two radio stations broadcast electromagnetic waves that both travel at 3.0 × 10^8 m/s in air. Station A transmits at 100 MHz and Station B at 200 MHz. Which comparison is correct?
options: Station B's waves have twice the wavelength of Station A's waves
Both stations' waves have equal wavelengths because their speed is equal
Station B's waves have half the wavelength of Station A's waves
Station B's waves travel twice as fast as Station A's waves
questions.explanation: Speed equals frequency × wavelength, so when the speed is fixed, frequency and wavelength are inversely related: doubling the frequency from 100 MHz to 200 MHz halves the wavelength from 3.0 m to 1.5 m. The tempting answer that Station B's waves travel twice as fast confuses frequency with speed — all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a given medium. The cue is to check what is held constant: here the speed is stated as the same for both, so only wavelength can change.

questions.stem: Which correctly states the Law of Conservation of Energy?
options: In a closed system the total energy stays the same; it is only transferred.
In a closed system energy is gradually used up, so the total falls.
In a closed system energy is destroyed by friction, so machines waste some.
In a closed system energy can be created by generators, never destroyed.
questions.explanation: Conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total amount in a closed system is constant, and transformations only change the form it takes. The idea that energy is 'used up' is the most tempting error, because energy does become less useful (usually spreading out as thermal energy), but the joules are still all present. The cue is to separate 'less useful' from 'less total' — degrading is not destroying. Generators do not create energy either; they transform kinetic energy into electrical energy.

questions.stem: How is the efficiency of an energy transformation calculated?
options: Wasted energy output divided by useful energy output, then multiplied by 100.
Useful energy output divided by wasted energy output, then multiplied by 100.
Useful energy output divided by total energy input, then multiplied by 100.
Total energy input divided by useful energy output, then multiplied by 100.
questions.explanation: Efficiency compares how much of the energy supplied ends up in the form you actually want, so it is useful output as a fraction of total input, expressed as a percentage. Dividing input by output is the most common slip, but that always gives a value above 100% for a real device, which should signal the ratio is upside down. Remember the answer must be no more than 100%, so the smaller number (useful output) goes on top.

questions.stem: An electric motor is supplied with 500 J of electrical energy and produces 350 J of useful kinetic energy. What is its efficiency, and what happens to the rest of the energy?
options: 143% efficient; the extra energy comes from the motion the motor generates.
30% efficient; the 350 J is the wasted energy and 150 J is the useful output.
70% efficient; the remaining 150 J is transformed mostly into thermal energy and sound.
70% efficient; the remaining 150 J is destroyed by resistance in the motor windings.
questions.explanation: Efficiency is 350 ÷ 500 × 100 = 70%, and conservation of energy means the missing 150 J must still exist — it has been transformed into thermal energy in the wires and bearings plus a little sound. Saying the 150 J is 'destroyed by resistance' gets the arithmetic right but breaks conservation; resistance transforms electrical energy to heat, it does not remove it. Always account for the leftover joules rather than deleting them.

questions.stem: Averaged over a year, Earth's surface and atmosphere stay at a roughly steady temperature. What does this imply about Earth's energy budget?
options: Earth absorbs more solar energy than it radiates, and stores the difference permanently in the oceans.
Earth radiates energy back to space at the same wavelengths as the sunlight it absorbs.
Earth destroys the surplus solar energy in the upper atmosphere so its temperature stays constant.
The energy Earth radiates to space as infrared each year is about equal to the solar energy it absorbs.
questions.explanation: A steady average temperature means input and output are balanced: absorbed solar radiation is matched by infrared radiation emitted to space, which is conservation of energy applied to the whole Earth system. The claim that Earth stores the surplus in the oceans is tempting because oceans do absorb heat, but continual net storage would mean a continually rising temperature, not a steady one. Note also that Earth emits mainly long-wavelength infrared because it is far cooler than the Sun.

questions.stem: Most energy transformations end with energy spread as heat. How does that fit conservation of energy?
options: The total afterwards is greater, since friction generates extra heat
The total energy afterwards equals the total before, but spread-out thermal energy is hard to use
The total afterwards is less, since heat is destroyed as it spreads
Heat is not counted, since only useful forms count
questions.explanation: Conservation of energy says energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed, so every joule of input can be accounted for in the outputs. Energy that becomes thermal energy spread thinly through the air and surroundings is described as 'degraded' or 'wasted' because it is impractical to recover, not because it has vanished. The tempting choice is that the total is less than before because the thermal energy is destroyed — this confuses 'unusable' with 'gone'. Cue: 'wasted energy' always means redirected to a non-useful output, never removed from the total.

questions.stem: A coal station burns coal to drive steam turbines. What are its useful and wasted outputs?
options: No wasted outputs, since conservation of energy says energy is conserved
Useful: electrical energy. Wasted: thermal energy in cooling water and flue gases
Useful: chemical energy in the coal. Wasted: the electricity sent out
Useful: thermal energy in the steam. Electricity is a by-product
questions.explanation: The useful output of a system is the form of energy the system is built to deliver — here, electricity — while wasted outputs are the forms released to the surroundings, mainly thermal energy in cooling water, exhaust gases and friction in the turbines. The tempting choice is that there are no wasted outputs because energy is conserved; conservation means the joules are all accounted for, but most of them still leave as unusable thermal energy. Cue: conservation is about the total, efficiency is about how much of that total is useful.

questions.stem: On a Sankey diagram for a petrol engine, what does the width of each arrow represent?
options: The time energy takes along that pathway during one engine cycle
The percentage wasted, with the same width used for every output
The quantity of energy on that pathway, drawn to scale against the input
The temperature reached by the engine part that pathway passes through
questions.explanation: In a Sankey diagram the arrow widths are drawn in proportion to the number of joules travelling by each route, so the widths of all the output arrows must add up to the width of the input arrow. That is exactly why the diagram makes conservation of energy visible at a glance. The tempting wrong answer refers to temperature — but a small amount of energy can raise a small mass to a high temperature, so temperature is not proportional to arrow width. Cue: Sankey widths measure joules, not degrees or seconds.

questions.stem: A rooftop solar panel receives 1200 J of light energy each second and produces 180 J of electrical energy each second. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: Efficiency is useful energy output divided by total energy input, expressed as a percentage: 180 ÷ 1200 = 0.15, or 15%. The tempting wrong answer of 85% comes from working out the wasted fraction (1020 ÷ 1200) instead of the useful fraction. Cue: the useful output always goes on top of the fraction, and the answer for a real device must be less than 100%.

questions.stem: Kettle A uses 250 kJ of electrical energy and delivers 200 kJ of useful thermal energy to the water. Kettle B uses 300 kJ and delivers 225 kJ to the water. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both kettles are equally efficient, because each wastes exactly the same 50 kJ of energy
Kettle A is more efficient at 125%, because its input is smaller than Kettle B's input
Kettle A is more efficient at 80%, even though Kettle B delivers more useful energy
Kettle B is more efficient at 75%, because it delivers more useful energy to the water
questions.explanation: Efficiency compares useful output with input: A gives 200 ÷ 250 = 80%, while B gives 225 ÷ 300 = 75%, so A is the more efficient kettle despite transferring fewer joules to the water. The tempting wrong answer picks B because it delivers more useful energy — but a bigger useful output from a much bigger input can still be a smaller fraction. Note also that A and B do not waste the same amount: A wastes 50 kJ and B wastes 75 kJ. Cue: efficiency is a ratio, so always compare fractions, not raw amounts.

questions.stem: A water pump is 60% efficient. How much electrical energy must be supplied for it to deliver 1.2 × 10^4 J of useful energy to the water?
questions.explanation: Since useful output = efficiency × input, the input is 1.2 × 10^4 ÷ 0.60 = 2.0 × 10^4 J, and the 0.8 × 10^4 J difference is wasted as thermal energy and sound. The tempting wrong answer of 0.72 × 10^4 J comes from multiplying by 0.60 instead of dividing, which would treat the useful output as the input. Cue: the input must always be the largest number in the calculation, so if your answer is smaller than the useful output, you have used the formula backwards.

questions.stem: In Earth's water cycle, what is the main energy input that drives the evaporation of water from the oceans?
options: Radiant energy from the Sun absorbed by the surface water of the oceans
Geothermal energy conducted upwards from Earth's hot core through the seabed
Gravitational potential energy stored in clouds high in the atmosphere
Kinetic energy supplied to the oceans by the daily rotation of the Earth
questions.explanation: The water cycle is a solar-powered Earth system: sunlight absorbed by ocean surfaces is transformed into the energy needed to change liquid water into vapour. Geothermal energy is a real but extremely small input to surface waters and is not what drives evaporation. Clouds only gain gravitational potential energy after evaporation has already lifted the water, so that option reverses the order of the transfers.

questions.stem: A clothes dryer is 85% efficient and is supplied with 40 kJ of electrical energy. How much energy is wasted?
options: 85 kJ
6 kJ
34 kJ
15 kJ
questions.explanation: Useful output is 0.85 × 40 kJ = 34 kJ, so the wasted energy is 40 − 34 = 6 kJ, which is 15% of the input. Choosing 34 kJ gives the useful output rather than the waste, which is the most common slip. Choosing 15 kJ comes from treating the 15% figure as kilojoules instead of applying it to the 40 kJ input.

questions.stem: In a hydroelectric power station, water stored high in a dam falls through pipes and spins turbines connected to generators. Which sequence correctly describes the main energy transformations?
options: Kinetic energy of water → gravitational potential energy → electrical energy in the turbines
Electrical energy of the generator → kinetic energy of turbines → potential energy of water
Chemical energy stored in water → kinetic energy of turbines → electrical energy
Gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy of water and turbines → electrical energy
questions.explanation: Water held behind a high dam has gravitational potential energy; as it falls this becomes kinetic energy, which the turbine and generator transform into electrical energy. The sequence starting with kinetic energy reverses the first two steps — water must be high before it can move fast downhill. Water is not a chemical fuel here, so no chemical energy is involved.

questions.stem: A household installs ceiling insulation and its winter heating bill falls sharply. Which statement best explains this in terms of energy transfers?
options: The insulation stops thermal energy transferring at all, so the rooms need no energy input once warmed
Less thermal energy escapes to the outside, so less energy input is needed to keep the rooms at the same temperature
The insulation creates extra thermal energy in the ceiling space, adding to the energy the heater supplies
The insulation raises the heater's efficiency above 100%, so the heater produces more energy than it uses
questions.explanation: Insulation reduces the rate at which thermal energy is transferred out of the house, so the heater has to replace less lost energy to maintain the same indoor temperature. The claim about efficiency above 100% is impossible — no device can output more energy than it is supplied. Insulation also only slows transfer; it never stops it completely, so a heated house always keeps losing some energy to the cold outside.

questions.stem: A power station transforms 35% of the chemical energy in its coal into electrical energy, and 90% of that electricity reaches homes after transmission losses. If 1000 MJ of coal is burnt, how much energy reaches homes?
options: 350 MJ
390 MJ
900 MJ
315 MJ
questions.explanation: The two stages multiply: 0.35 × 1000 MJ = 350 MJ generated, then 0.90 × 350 MJ = 315 MJ delivered. Choosing 350 MJ stops after the first stage and ignores transmission losses. Adding or averaging the percentages (as in 390 MJ) is not valid, because the second efficiency applies only to what survives the first stage.

questions.stem: A student tests a wind-up toy car. The spring stores 50 J. She measures 20 J of kinetic energy, 25 J of thermal energy in the gears and 3 J of sound — a total of 48 J. What is the best conclusion?
options: Exactly 2 J of energy was destroyed by friction in the gears, so the total afterwards is genuinely smaller
The law of conservation of energy applies only to electrical devices, so it does not apply to a wind-up toy
The spring must have stored only 48 J, because sound energy is not a real form of energy transfer
Energy was still conserved; about 2 J went to forms she did not measure, such as heating the air and the floor
questions.explanation: Conservation of energy means the totals must balance once every pathway is counted, and in a real experiment small amounts always escape unmeasured — thermal energy warming the air, the axles and the surface. The idea that 2 J was destroyed by friction is tempting, but friction transforms energy into thermal energy and sound rather than removing it. Sound is a genuine energy transfer, so discounting it does not fix the balance either.

questions.stem: Treating Earth as one energy system, what are its main energy input and output?
options: Input: radiation from the Sun. Output: infrared radiation emitted to space
Input: radiation from the Sun. Output: heat conducted into space through air
Input: heat from Earth's hot interior. Output: infrared radiation to space
Input: radiation from the Sun. Output: energy destroyed by clouds and oceans
questions.explanation: Almost all of the energy entering Earth's system arrives as solar radiation, and Earth loses energy only by radiating infrared back out through space, since radiation is the one transfer method that works across a vacuum. The option naming conduction through the air is tempting because conduction is a real transfer method, but space is essentially empty, so there are no particles to conduct energy away. Heat from Earth's interior is a genuine but very small contribution compared with sunlight, and energy is never destroyed — the cue is that a steady global temperature requires input and output to balance.

questions.stem: A blender is supplied with 800 J of electrical energy. It produces 480 J of useful kinetic energy in the blades and 60 J of sound. Assuming energy is conserved, how much thermal energy is produced?
questions.explanation: Conservation of energy means the outputs must add to the input: 800 − 480 − 60 = 260 J of thermal energy. Choosing 320 J is the common slip of subtracting only the useful kinetic energy and forgetting that the sound is also an output. The cue is to list every output and check that the total exactly equals the energy supplied.

questions.stem: A machine is 40% efficient and wastes 90 J of energy as heat and sound in one cycle. How much energy is supplied to it in that cycle?
questions.explanation: If the machine is 40% efficient then the wasted energy is the other 60% of the input, so input = 90 ÷ 0.60 = 225 J (giving 135 J useful). Choosing 225 J requires noticing that 90 J is the wasted share, not the useful share; the answer 150 J comes from treating 90 J as the 60%... in fact 225 J is the correct division, while 150 J results from mistakenly using 90 ÷ 0.6 as 90 ÷ 0.6 rounded wrongly or dividing by 0.4 after halving. The safest check is that useful plus wasted must equal the input: 135 + 90 = 225 J.

questions.stem: In a grassland food chain, only about 10% of the energy stored in the grass ends up stored in the kangaroos that eat it. Which statement correctly applies the Law of Conservation of Energy to this transfer?
options: The other 90% is destroyed during digestion, which is why energy must be constantly resupplied to ecosystems by the Sun
The other 90% is recycled directly back into the grass by the kangaroos, so the overall ecosystem transfer is 100% efficient
The other 90% is converted into new matter inside the kangaroo, so the energy total is smaller but the mass total is larger
The other 90% is not destroyed; it leaves the food chain mainly as thermal energy from respiration and as energy in undigested wastes
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so if only 10% of the input is stored as new body tissue, the remaining 90% must still be accounted for — it is transferred out of the food chain as heat released by respiration and movement, and as chemical energy in faeces and other wastes. The option saying the energy is destroyed during digestion is the most tempting, because the energy really does disappear from the food chain, but 'lost from a system' never means 'destroyed' — it means transferred somewhere less useful. When you see a low efficiency figure, always ask where the wasted energy went, not whether it vanished.

questions.stem: What does the law of conservation of energy state?
options: Energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred
Energy is gradually used up whenever work is done
Energy can be created if a large enough force is applied
Energy always increases inside a closed system
questions.explanation: Energy changes form and moves between objects, but the total never changes. Saying it is 'used up' is the common phrasing and it is wrong — the energy is still there, usually spread out as heat.
questions.teaching:
The everyday phrase "using up energy" is misleading, and this law is the correction to it.

Follow the energy through a bike ride. Chemical energy from your breakfast becomes movement; the movement gradually becomes warmth in the brake blocks, the tyres and the surrounding air. Add every form together at the end and the total matches what you began with — nothing has gone missing. What has changed is how useful it is. Concentrated energy in food is easy to do work with; the same quantity spread thinly through the atmosphere is not. So "wasted" energy has not vanished, it has become too dilute to use. Any machine claiming to put out more than it takes in is claiming something this law forbids.

questions.stem: How is energy transferred by conduction?
options: By a chemical reaction inside a material
Through direct contact between particles
By waves travelling through empty space
By a heated fluid rising and circulating
questions.explanation: In conduction, vibrating particles knock into their neighbours and pass energy along, so the material must be in contact. Convection is the tempting answer, but that needs a fluid that can move and carry energy with it.
questions.teaching:
Heat moves in three distinct ways, and each has a requirement that rules it in or out. Sorting them by what they need is the quickest way to tell them apart.

The one asked about here needs the material to be touching, because it works by particles vibrating and jostling their neighbours along a chain. That is why a metal spoon in hot tea heats along its length, and why metals do it best — their free electrons carry energy faster than vibration alone. The second method needs a fluid that can flow and carry warm material bodily. The third needs nothing at all, which is how sunlight crosses empty space.

questions.stem: Which type of energy transfer needs no material at all?
options: Conduction
Convection
None of these travel through space
Radiation
questions.explanation: Radiation travels as electromagnetic waves and crosses a vacuum, which is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth. Conduction and convection both need particles, so neither works through empty space.
questions.teaching:
Two of the three heat-transfer methods depend entirely on particles: one passes vibration along a chain of touching particles, the other physically moves heated fluid around.

Both fail in a vacuum. Yet the Sun heats the Earth across 150 million kilometres of near-empty space, so a third route must exist. That route is electromagnetic waves, which need no medium whatsoever — the same family of waves as visible light, just at longer wavelengths. It is also why a vacuum flask works: the gap between its walls removes the first two methods, and the silvered surfaces reflect the third back.

questions.stem: What kind of energy does a moving object have?
options: Kinetic energy
Gravitational potential energy
Chemical energy
Elastic potential energy
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is energy of motion, and it grows with both mass and speed. Gravitational potential energy is the tempting answer, but that depends on height, not on whether the object is moving.
questions.teaching:
Energy comes in stores, and naming the right one usually means asking what condition the object is in right now.

If it is raised up high, the store depends on its height and is released when it falls. If it is stretched or compressed, the store depends on the deformation. If it is moving, the store depends on mass and speed — and speed is squared in the formula, so doubling the speed quadruples this store. That squaring is why stopping distances grow so sharply with speed, and why a car at 60 km/h carries four times the energy it does at 30.

questions.stem: What does a wave transfer from place to place?
options: Mass
Temperature
Energy
Matter
questions.explanation: A wave carries energy while the material it travels through only vibrates in place. Thinking matter travels is the usual mistake — a floating cork bobs up and down as a wave passes rather than moving along with it.
questions.teaching:
Watch a cork on a pond as ripples pass. It bobs up and down but does not travel across the pond with the ripples. That single observation is the whole idea.

The water is not moving from one side to the other; the disturbance is. What travels is the pattern, and with it the ability to do work at the far end — enough to rock the cork, or in a large enough wave to knock you over. The same holds for sound, where air molecules vibrate about fixed positions, and for light. So the medium stays put on average while something else moves through it.

questions.stem: What is the frequency of a wave?
options: The distance between two neighbouring peaks
The height of a wave above its resting position
The speed at which the wave travels
The number of waves passing a point each second
questions.explanation: Frequency counts waves per second, measured in hertz. Wavelength is the tempting confusion: that is the distance between peaks, which is a length rather than a count.
questions.teaching:
Several wave measurements sound similar, so it helps to notice which are counts and which are lengths.

Wavelength is a distance, from one crest to the next, measured in metres. Amplitude is also a distance, from the resting position out to a crest. The quantity in this question is different in kind: it is a count of how many complete waves go past a fixed point in one second, measured in hertz. In sound it corresponds to pitch — a higher count is a higher note. The three link together, since wave speed equals this count multiplied by wavelength.

questions.stem: Where does wasted energy in a machine usually end up?
options: As heat and sound in the surroundings
Destroyed completely by friction and air resistance
Stored inside the machine for use later on
Converted back into useful energy again
questions.explanation: Wasted energy is still energy: friction and vibration spread it into the surroundings as heat and sound. Saying friction destroys it is the common error, and it would break conservation of energy.
questions.teaching:
Start from the rule that energy cannot be destroyed. Whatever a machine does not turn into useful output has to still exist somewhere, so the question is where it goes.

Almost always, friction and vibration spread it into the surroundings — the motor housing warms, the gears whine, the air around it heats very slightly. It has not disappeared, and no machine has destroyed it. What has changed is that it is now thinly spread and at a low temperature, which makes it effectively impossible to use for anything. That is what "wasted" really means: dispersed, not gone.

questions.stem: What does it mean if a machine is 80% efficient?
options: The machine runs for 80% of the time without stopping
The machine wastes 80% of the energy supplied
The machine needs 80% less energy than others
80% of the energy supplied becomes useful output
questions.explanation: Efficiency is the share of supplied energy that comes out useful, so 80% useful means 20% wasted. Reading it as the wasted share is the usual reversal, and it is worth checking which way round a question asks.
questions.teaching:
Efficiency compares two quantities: how much energy goes in, and how much of it comes out doing the job you wanted.

Expressed as a percentage, it is the useful share. The rest is not destroyed — it leaves as heat, sound or vibration. So a figure like this tells you directly what fraction is useful, and subtracting from 100 tells you what fraction is wasted. The commonest error is reading the number as the wasted share instead, which reverses the meaning entirely. Read the question carefully and check which of the two it is asking for, because both numbers are available from the one figure.

questions.stem: What is the unit of energy?
options: The volt
The joule
The newton
The watt
questions.explanation: Energy is measured in joules. The watt is the tempting choice, but that measures power — joules per second — which is a rate rather than an amount.
questions.teaching:
Energy and power are different quantities and have different units, and mixing them up is the most common slip in this topic.

Energy is an amount — a total, like litres of water. Power is a rate — how fast that amount is delivered or used, like litres per second. So the unit of power is defined as one unit of energy per second. A 2000 W kettle uses energy twice as fast as a 1000 W one, but if the second runs for twice as long, both use the same total. Electricity bills are in kilowatt-hours, which is a power multiplied by a time, and is therefore a measure of energy rather than power.

questions.stem: What is the amplitude of a wave?
options: The distance between two neighbouring peaks
The number of waves passing each second
The speed at which the wave travels
The height of a wave from its rest position
questions.explanation: Amplitude measures how far the medium moves from rest, and it corresponds to loudness in sound or brightness in light. Distance between peaks is wavelength, which is the usual mix-up.
questions.teaching:
A wave has several measurements attached to it and they are easy to muddle, because they all sound like sizes.

Picture a rope being shaken up and down. One measurement is how far the rope swings away from its undisturbed line — measure that and you are measuring how much energy the wave is carrying. In sound it corresponds to loudness; in light, to brightness. A different measurement is the distance from one crest to the next, which is the wavelength. A third counts how many waves pass a fixed point each second, which is the frequency. Turning up the volume on a speaker changes the first while leaving the third alone; playing a higher note changes the third.

questions.stem: What kind of wave is sound?
options: Electromagnetic
Stationary
Longitudinal
Transverse
questions.explanation: Sound is longitudinal: the air vibrates back and forth along the direction the wave travels. That is also why sound needs a medium and cannot cross a vacuum.
questions.teaching:
Waves are classified by the direction the medium vibrates compared with the direction the wave travels, and there are two possibilities.

In one, the vibration is at right angles to the travel direction — think of shaking a rope up and down while the wave runs along it. In the other, the vibration is back and forth along the same line the wave moves, so the medium is alternately squashed and stretched. A slinky pushed and pulled from one end shows the second type clearly, with visible bands of compression running along it. Sound behaves that second way: air molecules move back and forth along the direction the sound travels, creating pressure variations your eardrum detects.

questions.stem: What kind of wave is light?
options: Longitudinal
A sound wave
A pressure wave
Transverse
questions.explanation: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, vibrating at right angles to its direction of travel. Being electromagnetic is also why it crosses empty space where sound cannot.
questions.teaching:
Light belongs to the electromagnetic family, along with radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All of them are the same kind of wave at different wavelengths.

What vibrates is not a material at all but electric and magnetic fields, oscillating at right angles to the direction of travel. That perpendicular oscillation puts light in the same category as a wave on a rope rather than the same category as sound. It has one practical consequence worth knowing: because the vibration has a direction across the beam, light can be filtered by orientation, which is exactly how polarised sunglasses cut glare off water.

questions.stem: What is the energy stored in a stretched spring called?
options: Elastic potential energy
Kinetic energy
Chemical energy
Nuclear energy
questions.explanation: Stretching or compressing a spring stores elastic potential energy, released when it springs back. Kinetic energy is the tempting answer, but that requires the object to be moving.
questions.teaching:
Stores of energy are named for the condition that holds them. Position in a gravitational field gives one kind; movement gives another; chemical bonds give a third.

Stretching or squashing something that springs back is a fourth. The energy went in as work against the material's resistance, it is held while the deformation lasts, and it comes back out when the object is released — which is what makes a bow, a trampoline and a wind-up toy work. Note that it needs no motion at all: a stretched rubber band sitting still is holding energy, which is why calling it a movement store is the tempting mistake.

questions.stem: Why can we hear no sound in space?
options: Sound is absorbed by nearby stars
There are no particles to carry the vibration
Sound waves travel too slowly to arrive
Space is too cold for sound to exist
questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium, and space is close enough to empty that there is nothing to vibrate. Light reaches us from the same place because electromagnetic waves need no medium at all.
questions.teaching:
It follows from what sound actually is: a pattern of compressions travelling through a material. Something has to be there to be compressed.

Space is close enough to empty that there is essentially nothing to carry the vibration, so no sound can propagate at all — a vacuum is silence by definition. Light behaves completely differently, which is the useful contrast: it is an electromagnetic wave, needs no medium, and crosses the vacuum happily. That is why you can see an explosion in space but could never hear it, and why films that include the sound are getting the physics wrong for dramatic effect.
